title: Values, types and a first calculator
summary: Start the calculator project: variables and types, reading input, arithmetic operators, integer vs floating-point division, and making decisions.

steps.title: Variables have types
hints: Print each part with `<<`: `std::cout << a << " + " << b << " = " << a + b << '\n';`

steps.title: Reading input
hints: `std::cin >> a >> b;` reads two whitespace-separated numbers into `a` and `b`.

quiz.question: `int a = 7; int b = 2;` — what is the value of `a / b`?
options: It doesn't compile: the result isn't a whole number.
explanations: That's what Python 3's `/` gives you. In C++, the *types* of the operands decide which division happens.

Right: `int / int` is **integer division** — the fractional part is discarded (truncated toward zero). Python spells this `//`. To get 3.5 you need at least one operand to be floating-point: `7.0 / 2` or `static_cast<double>(a) / b`.
Integer division doesn't round — it truncates toward zero. `7 / 2` is 3, and `-7 / 2` is -3.
It compiles fine. C++ picks integer division because both operands are `int`. That's a classic source of silent bugs.

steps.title: All four operations
hints: Four `std::cout` lines, one per operator: `+ - * /`. Because `a` and `b` are `double`, `/` is floating-point division.

steps.title: Challenge: an expression calculator
hints: A single character has type `char`. `std::cin >> a >> op >> b;` reads `3 * 4` into three variables, skipping the spaces.
Compare characters with single quotes: `if (op == '+')`. A `switch (op)` with `case '+':` is a tidy alternative — don't forget `break;`.
Check for division by zero *before* dividing. (For doubles, `1.0 / 0` doesn't crash — it produces `inf`. That's still not what a user wants to see.)
